primitives.name: Outer Approximation Duality
primitives.verbatim_quote: (3c) If μ is a finite measure defined on the class of Borel subsets of a metric space X, and U is the class of open subsets of X, then μ(E) = inf {μ(U): E ⊂ U ε U} for every Borel set E.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'E': 'Borel set, dimensionless', 'U': 'Open set, dimensionless', '\\mu': 'Finite measure, [measure]', '\\mathcal{U}': 'Class of open subsets, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: X is a metric space, μ is a finite measure on Borel sets, E is a Borel set.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When E lacks finite measure or X is not metrizable.

layer2.mapping: GSI employs outer approximation to define consistent probability distributions over Borel sets; GSE uses it for deterministic state transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Consistency of μ(E) across open superset approximations.

primitives.name: Measure Agreement on Open Sets
primitives.verbatim_quote: Apply 5.2, 8.5, and 13.A.) (3b) If two finite measures μ and v are defined on the class of Borel subsets of a metric space X and agree on the class U of open subsets of X, then they agree for all Borel sets.

primitives.assumptions: X is a metric space, μ, v are finite measures, U is class of open sets.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When μ and v differ on open sets or X is not separable.

layer2.mapping: GSI derives full measure agreement from open-set agreement; GSE uses it to validate state transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Equality of μ(E) and v(E) for all Borel sets when restricted to open sets.

The core insight lies in the interplay between outer and inner approximations of Borel sets through finite measures. Outer approximation (3c) expresses μ(E) as the infimum over open supersets, while inner approximation (3d) expresses it as the supremum over closed subsets. These dual formulations ensure that any Borel set can be consistently measured from both directions. The agreement of two finite measures on open sets (3b) implies their equivalence on all Borel sets—a foundational result for measure theory. This duality enables robust probabilistic inference in GSI and deterministic state evolution in GSE. Failure occurs when sets lack finite measure or when the underlying space lacks sufficient structure (e.g., non-metrizable).
